mods.name: Bob's Pipes
mods.description: Bob's Pipes: a reusable carved corewood pipe, made at the workbench. Prepare Meadow, Honeywood or Cloudberry pipe tobacco at Quad's Cigar Rolling Table. Use a tin to pack an empty pipe, then use your hotbar pipe near a burning fire or holding a torch to light it. Use it again to put it out and save the unfinished bowl. The lit pipe rests in your mouth, with a small ember, quiet smoke, occasional exhalations and a slowly seasoned finish. Combat, swimming and exposed rain put it away. Small blend bonuses, configurable down to cosmetic only. Requires Quad's Cigars; with its smoking API (v1 or newer), pipes and cigars share one active smoke.
mods.notes: 0.1.6: no error every frame after leaving a world with a pipe lit (the smoker had gone with the world).
mods.restart: Adds saved pipe and tobacco item prefabs. Install Bob's Pipes and Quad's Cigars on the host and every player, then restart Valheim before loading the world.

mods.name: BuildKit
mods.description:
Norse building pieces for the hammer (Building tab, at a workbench).

Turf roofs: sod on birch bark over boards, in every shape the game's wooden roofs come in (26° and 45°: straight, ridge, outer and inner corner). Each one snaps, holds and wears exactly like the wooden roof it's shaped on, so the two mix freely. The grass is the game's own (from its unused turf roof) and sways in the wind. Open edges tear: the sod reaches out in lumps and droops over the edge, with sticks poking out of the soil. Sides that meet another roof piece stay clean, so a long roof shows no seams. A turf roof keeps the house warm: +1 comfort when you're sheltered under one (once, however many pieces). 2 wood and 1 fine wood (birch: its bark).

Smoke-hole roofs (26° and 45°), for single-slope roofs: a turf roof with a metre-square hole through it and a little hooded vent over the hole, as a longhouse without a chimney let out its hearth's smoke. Put it over the fire: the smoke rises up the hole and rolls out under the hood, and the hood keeps the rain off the fire below. 4 wood and 1 fine wood.

Turf ridge smoke vents (26° and 45°): a ridge piece with a slot open along its whole length and a single-pitch hood over it. A house's smoke gathers all along under its ridge, so put them in the ridge right over the hearth: the smoke rises out under the hood, the hood keeps the rain off the fire. Keep the slot clear (no ridge log over it). 4 wood and 1 fine wood.

Reloads in a world. Native Linux and Windows.
mods.notes: 0.3.0: the shingle roofs, the dragon ridge ends and the stave wall, post and portal are gone: the game has its own (the darkwood roofs, the dragon and raven carvings, the Deep North's stave set). Any of them standing in a world disappear. The wattle and daub wall no longer shows the sky in thin cracks round its clay: the panels now run into the timbers.

mods.name: BuildShapes
mods.description:
Draw curves, loops, circles, arches and straight runs of beams or walls, rows of posts or decorations with gaps, and mirror pieces as shared BuildOrders ghosts. Requires BuildOrders with its planning and ghost-selection APIs. Hallwright (timber halls, longhouses, stave temples) is its own mod since BuildShapes 0.9.0: install Hallwright for the stake.

Pick a piece in the hammer as usual, then hold Left Ctrl (about a third of a second, without clicking or scrolling) for the shape radial: flick towards Curve, Arch, Circle or Mirror and let go (or click). It looks like the game's own radial; it shows only the shapes that work with the piece in your hand, and Build leaves the shape tool. Escape, or letting go in the middle, closes it.

In a shape tool: left click places markers; once they're all down, the shape shows as a sketch (below). Scroll rolls them about their length and Shift+scroll turns each about its own up (in the game's 22.5° steps), E plans them as shared ghosts (and uses nothing you're looking at), Delete clears the shape and keeps the tool, Backspace removes the last marker, U removes your last shape's unbuilt ghosts, and Escape leaves the tool. Ctrl+scroll sets how round a Curve is, an Arch's height and a Circle's plane; Ctrl+Shift+scroll sets the gap between pieces (none, or up to 16 m, shrunk evenly so the outer pieces still meet the ends: a row of posts, torches or banners along the curve, as Repeat used to do). Ctrl+click selects pieces in Mirror; a slow Ctrl+click or Ctrl+scroll that opens the radial still does what it would have done.

Curve: pick any piece with a length (a beam, pole, stone block, wall or pillar) and click points: two make a straight line (at any slope, or upright), a third and more a curve through them all in the order you clicked (up to 64). Click the first point again to close the loop; it becomes just another point on the curve. E plans at any point, Backspace removes the last point (or opens the loop), Delete starts over. Ctrl+scroll sets how round it runs through its points, 100% down to 0%: at 0% the sides are straight with sharp corners and pieces end exactly at each corner. Home switches how pieces follow it: along the curve in 3D (beams, pillars) or upright, standing plumb and turning to follow it, by the bottom of their ends, at the lower end's height on a slope (walls, fences); a pole or pillar stands side by side instead, upright, spaced by its width along the curve (a palisade). Walls, poles and pillars start standing; Home lays them along the curve (stacked poles for a tall post). Pieces are laid end to end along their own length: the axis their snap points spread furthest along (a stone block lies along the path; a pillar along its height), or their mesh's longest side; 0.1–8 metres long, native length, overlaps spread evenly. Two points replace the old Line tool.

Arch: pick a piece with a length and click both ends: the circle through both ends and its top, its ends leaning as the circle has them (a half-circle stands up at its ends). Ctrl+scroll sets the height above the ends' middle (0–32 m); a gold guide marks the top. Unequal end heights work; the ends must be apart horizontally. (It was Arc before 0.13.0.)

Circle: click the centre, then a point on the edge. The circle lies in the plane through both points, tilted only as much as they need; Ctrl+scroll snaps it level (at the edge's height) or stands it upright through both points (a ring on a wall). Its pieces go evenly all the way round; Home, roll, turn and gaps work as in Curve.

Mirror: click two points for a vertical mirror plane, then Ctrl+click built pieces or visible ghosts to toggle source selection. Thin wire boxes show sources; the mirrored copies show as real pieces. Ctrl+Backspace removes the last selection. Reflection axes and pivot compensation follow native snap layouts, fixing triangular under-roof walls and sloped beams while preserving ordinary roof pitch; mesh bounds are a fallback. Asymmetric carvings and handed meshes keep their original geometry, so inspect the ghosts before building.

Live draft sharing: other players with BuildShapes see your markers and shape previews as cyan visuals labeled with your name. Sharing is on by default; F7 exposes send/receive and piece-preview toggles under Shared drafts. These visuals have no colliders, costs or build actions; E still creates normal shared BuildOrders ghosts. Drafts clear on submission/exit/unload and expire after disconnects. Viewers draw the nearest four drafts within 120 m, with at most 4,096 shared pieces visible.

Sketch preview (the default): the shape is drawn like an architect's watercolour, as Hallwright drafts are: pen strokes along every edge where a piece folds or ends, over a wash of the piece's own colour on watercolour-paper grain. It draws itself in along the shape, ink first, when it's first complete; turning or reshaping it afterwards shows at once. PreviewStyle (F7, General) = Pieces shows the real pieces instead. Either way previews are local only (no colliders, no cost). While a shape tool is out, its keys stand in for the game's key hints along the bottom of the screen, in the same look, with a line above for the shape, its markers and its settings. Curves and circles are limited to 256 metres round, Arch to 128, and every shape to 256 pieces. Markers/sources require 40-metre reach; the planner checks all output positions, recipes, wards, and no-build areas. Scaled and terrain-operation pieces are excluded. Selections are pose snapshots.

Shapes never change terrain; built pieces stay intact and normal materials/support still apply. Undo is one submitted shape across all tools and clears on death, world change, or F6. Only the designer needs BuildShapes; participating players should use updated BuildOrders and the selected pieces. Keys are in F7 (Controls): ShapeMenu (Left Ctrl), ConfirmShape (E). ClaudeTools: shapes radial [wedge|off] holds the radial open, and shapes hints <tool|off> [full] shows a tool's key hints, for pictures.
mods.notes: 0.13.2: The status line above a shape tool's keys no longer logs a missing-font warning each time it's built.

mods.name: Hallwright
mods.description:
Design a whole Viking timber hall, Norse longhouse, stave temple, mountain cabin, stilt cabin or stone keep from a floor plan you stake out on the ground, and plan it as shared BuildOrders ghosts. Requires BuildOrders with its planning API. Hallwright was part of BuildShapes until BuildShapes 0.8.10: update BuildShapes to 0.9.0 or newer with it, or both mods put a stake in the hammer's menu. Saved drafts, ground records and your Hallwright, key and shared-draft settings carry over.

Hallwright stake: pick the stake in the hammer's build menu (Misc) and Hallwright is on. Click the ground for each corner (its ghost stands where the snapped corner will go), Shift+click an entrance, Ctrl+click a smoke hole or chimney (Shift/Ctrl+Backspace removes the last), and press E inside the outline for the settings. L also opens the settings. Picking another piece keeps the draft; picking the stake again reopens it, with the saved draft for this character and world. The stake is free and never built.

Sketch preview (the default): the draft is drawn like an architect's watercolour, in the manner of Piranesi. Each piece is inked along the edges where its surface folds and where it ends, in pen strokes that run past the corners, bend a little and now and then go over a line twice, over a wash of the piece's own colour (timber brown, thatch straw, stone grey) softened towards the paper, on watercolour-paper grain, each piece's wash a little different. Faint construction lines carry the hall's floor, wall tops, eaves and ridge a little past its corners and gables, roofs light as clean slopes, and markers are drawn in blue pencil. New pieces draw themselves in, bottom up, ink first, then the colour washes in: the whole hall when it first takes shape, only the added pieces when you change a setting. It's solid, and the sun, shade and fog fall on it as on the world around it. Pieces the support estimate says would fall are inked red on pink. Materials and Ghosts show the real pieces; Layout shows only the guides. ClaudeTools: hall options preview=sketch|materials|ghosts|layout.

Drawing: click square corners in boundary order with the stake. The first edge sets the rotated 2-metre grid, turned to the nearest of the game's 22.5° build steps (FreeAngle in the config allows any angle); subsequent edges snap to its two directions. Concave L/U outlines work. While you draw, dotted lines on the ground follow the terrain between corners, a live line shows where the next click would land (and the way back to the first corner), and each line's length floats above it. Press E inside the outline (or L) for the settings, or click the first corner again to finish drawing. Backspace removes a corner; Delete clears the outline. From four corners onward, an invalid outline automatically shows its reason at the centre of the screen while drawing. Adjust walls (2–4 m), roof pitch (26°/45°), Gabled/Tiered silhouette, entrance type and edge, foundation lift and an intricacy dial (Simple, Crafted, Ornate, Grand, King’s hall). Exact foundation lift and fine nudges have numeric controls. The shell previews using the real meshes, as a Sketch (below), Materials or Ghosts, with a roof visibility button. Auto entrances use an unlocked 3 m gate when wall height is 4 m or taller; choose Door or Gate explicitly. Gates require at least 4 m walls, so no beam crosses the top of the gate. The opening and header fit the actual native piece height. Tiered roofs raise the central roof by 1 m above low side aisles on wings at least 6 m wide; matching gables, vertical roof-step walls, shaped rafters and structural inner colonnades support the raised tier. Narrow wings stay gabled. Its floors, exterior walls and entrance, joined rectangular roof wings, gable infill, trusses, terrain-reaching foundations and entrance steps are fitted together. Small odd-width gable peaks are intentionally vented. Intricacy adds knee braces, radiating gable timberwork, darkwood arches and raven crests when unlocked.

Longhouse details: toggle Deep roof overhangs, Covered entrance porch, and Sweeping gable timberwork independently. Overhangs extend 2 m with native 26° eave aprons (a 1 m drop) and bracket/outrigger beams; extensions that overlap another wing or the porch are skipped. Walls at least 3 m high preserve 2 m under the side apron. The 4 × 2 m porch needs a straight entrance edge at least 4 m long and clear space outside, adds 8 m² of deck, uses normal floor/roof pieces and braces, and brings its foundations to the terrain. The floor height also samples the porch; entrance steps start at the porch's outer edge. Swept exposed gables at least 4 m wide use curved paths of native 1 m beams with overlapping joints. Ridge ends offer Auto/None/Dragon/Raven: Auto adds an unlocked native carving at Ornate and above, explicit Dragon/Raven require their recipe unlocked, and carvings face outward where they clear other wings. All added pieces contribute their normal material costs and support checks; unresolved collapses still block planning.

Mark entrances: after drawing a Hallwright outline, Shift+click near an exterior wall for each desired doorway (up to eight). The solver snaps within 4 m to metre positions and jointly preserves clear openings, interior stairs and external decks. Preview outlines show fitted door positions. Shift+click a marker again or Shift+Backspace removes it; options also list removals. The first marker gets the covered porch and sets the basement entrance ground height. All marked doors use the selected Door/Gate setting. Each receives stairs or a cellar deck and apron. With no entrance markers, the original entrance-edge selector remains available. ClaudeTools: hall doors <x,z>... or hall doors clear; hall entrances checks native built passage clearance.

Windows and chimneys: Shuttered windows (on by default) fill every other wall panel with a pair of native wooden window shutters (bronze nails needed). Ctrl+click a floor tile to put a chimney above it: the roof opens there and a timber flue rises past the ridge, with a shaft through any upper storeys. Light your fire under it. Up to four; Ctrl+click again or Ctrl+Backspace removes one.

Layout guides: terrain-height corner markers have amber posts at least 4 m tall, extending to taller planned walls. Floor and storey outlines show the boundary, with ridge/gable guides following the roof settings. In Layout preview the corner posts show through terrain and buildings, with outline guides for the building volume; with Sketch, Materials or Ghosts the pieces show the volume, the posts hide behind them and the outlines are left out. Select Sketch, Materials, Ghosts or Layout in Hallwright options. Door markers have tall posts too. Guides have no collision or piece cost and can be shared with other Hallwright players.

Longhouse (Norse): choose Longhouse in the settings' style row for a hall built the way the Norse built theirs. The floor is dug into the ground (0.5 m below the average ground by default, up to 2 m), a strip 1.5 m wide dug along the outside of the walls and a ramp down to each door; nothing is heaped up. A long hearth of the game's hearths runs down the middle aisle, with smoke holes in the roof beside the fires (never above them), as the Norse had no chimneys; each is left open to let the smoke out. A stone footing (two courses of the game's stone fence under a half-height timber wall) is on by default. Raised platforms line the long walls (2 m deep from 10 m wide, 1 m at 8 m), two rows of aisle posts carry the roof instead of low tie beams (one roof up to 10 m wide, even in plain wood), the door sits near one end of the longest wall, and walls default to 2 m. Each feature has a switch. The ground changes only at Plan shell (dug ground is painted as dirt); once the hall is taken down, Restore ground in the options puts it back, leaving alone anything changed since. Removing the hall's plan (BuildOrders' Plans window, or U) puts the ground back by itself when nothing of it is built there.

Hallwright now supports one to three storeys and an optional 3 m stone basement. Interior native stairs have landings, clear headroom openings and guards; structural columns avoid the walking route. A straight flight needs 2 × 8/10/12 m including landings for 2/3/4 m storeys. Concave floors and roofs stay within the drawn cell union. High intricacy adds daylight windows, carved bands and King’s hall knotwork with unlocked darkwood panels. All native pieces count toward materials, support and the 2,048-piece shell limit.

Basement checkbox: stone slabs and retaining walls below the main floor, interior stairs, entrance deck and a level apron with the ground floor just above the outside entrance terrain. Previewing changes no ground. Plan shell excavates the footprint (plus retaining-wall clearance) and grades the entrance before adding shared ghosts; failed submission restores it. Choose a clear, dry, loaded site within native 8 m digging limits. Requires unlocked stone walls/floors and wooden stairs. Confirmation acquires loaded terrain through the native ownership API and refreshes/rechecks it before excavation; restoration does the same after validating access and saved heights. You can plan while joining another player. Ownership changes mid-operation stop the edit and retain recovery.

U only removes unbuilt ghosts. Restore ground in Hallwright options restores the saved excavation after clearing any built cellar; it refuses overlapping later edits or existing buildings. Recovery survives F6/restarts in one per-world record under BepInEx/config. Keep excavation discards that record and allows another cellar. Reopen Hallwright to find recovery even without drawing another outline. The updated planner PR retains completed add-on records for Takedown. ClaudeTools: hall options storeys=1|2|3 basement=on|off detail=0..4; hall stairs/pieces inspect native built pieces; hall restoreground/keepground are explicit terrain actions.

Materials default to Auto, based on your character's known hammer recipes. Stronger core-wood posts, stone plinths, darkwood details and reinforced ridge supports are used only when unlocked. Select Timber/Core wood/Stone base/Darkwood to restrict the style. A live normal-cost materials bill and station list accompany the preview. Unlock changes refresh automatically. Foundations raise the floor above the highest sampled ground; terrain stays intact unless Basement is selected; existing pieces are never removed. Native collider contacts, actual material support losses and nearby built supports estimate whether the complete shell stands; extra interior ridge columns are added when necessary, and unresolved collapsing pieces block acceptance. Confirm rechecks the current terrain, support and unlocks, then creates one shared ghost plan and returns to normal building. This estimate is not a substitute for the game's final placement checks.

Hallwright supports 24 corners, 256 floor tiles (1,024 m²), corners up to 64 m along either grid axis from the first corner, 12 roof wings and 2,048 pieces including foundations, within 70 m of the designer. Long ridges span the complete outline instead of splitting at 24 m; roof width still follows unlocked structural materials. The piece budget remains separate: large or tall ornate halls may need lower intricacy. Move toward the centre before confirming a large outline. Diagonal/self-crossing outlines, unloaded or protected ground, excessive foundations and stretched beams are rejected. Large shells need BuildOrders' TryCreateBuildingShell API (provided in the Hallwright planner PR); older planners can accept shells up to their 256-piece cap. U removes the last plan's unbuilt ghosts; pick the stake again after confirming to use U. Local preview state clears on F6, death or world changes; an unsubmitted draft reopens from its saved copy when you pick the stake again. ClaudeTools exposes hall catalog/rectangle/outline/options/status/resume/ui/clear/confirm/undo and a hallpreview camera frame for testing.

Stave temple: stake out the floor plan, open the settings and choose Stave temple in the style row. The solver fits a tall central chamber into the outline, with lower surrounding roofs and one or two narrowing tower crowns. Each upper tower has an aperture through the roof below, preserving an open interior. Concave outlines work when they have room for the rectangular chamber; the remaining wings stay inside the drawn footprint and get passages into the chamber.

Choose 4 / 6 / 8 m chamber height, one / two tower crowns, and Open surrounding galleries. Galleries reserve a 2 m covered walk around the chamber, with low outer rails; turning them off encloses the side rooms. Keep the chamber at least 2 m taller than the side wings. One crown needs a 6 m-wide chamber: start with at least 10 × 10 m when galleries are on. Two crowns need a 10 m-wide chamber, core-wood framing and at least 14 × 14 m with galleries. A 14 × 18 m outline is a good first design. Too-small outlines explain which setting to change.

Intricacy, roof pitch, layered eaves, swept gable beams, porch and native dragon/raven carvings use the existing controls. Auto uses unlocked materials, including reinforced timber for tall staves. Columns avoid the doorways and central aisle; native support estimates still block unstable plans. Plan shell creates one normal-cost BuildOrders plan, subject to the existing 2,048-piece budget. Temple outlines/settings use saved Hallwright drafts and live draft sharing. This style is a single open chamber; choose Longhouse for storeys or a basement. ClaudeTools supports `hall options style=temple chamber=6 crowns=1 gallery=on`, and status reports the solved chamber and tower height.

Saved Hallwright drafts: outlines, entrance hints and settings auto-save per character and world. Picking the stake again reopens the local preview after F6, restarting or exiting. Reopening changes no terrain or shared plans; terrain/support/recipes are checked again. Delete, or Clear draft in the settings window, clears the outline and saved draft; successful Plan shell removes the saved draft. Drawing pauses during a planner-only reload or another planner menu, preserving markers. Large-shell capability is checked before basement excavation.

Live draft sharing: other players with Hallwright see your corner posts, outline, roof/storey guides and piece previews as cyan visuals labeled with your name. Sharing is on by default. The settings offer Share my draft and Include piece previews; F7 exposes send/receive and piece-preview toggles under Shared drafts. Layout sends only guides and hidden roofs stay hidden. These visuals have no colliders, terrain effects, costs or build actions; Plan shell still creates normal shared BuildOrders ghosts. Drafts clear on submission/exit/unload and expire after disconnects. Viewers draw the nearest four drafts within 120 m, with at most 4,096 shared pieces visible; turn off piece previews for guides alone. Only designers need Hallwright for submitted BuildOrders plans, but live drafts require it on designer and viewer (BuildShapes players don't see hall drafts).

Cabins and keeps: three more styles for the cold and the wet. Mountain cabin: walls of stacked core-wood logs whose ends cross half a metre past the corners, logs halfway up the gables, reaching the roof, boards above them, two courses of fieldstone fence under them with a dressed stone at each corner, a steep 67° roof that sheds snow, and a fire pit under a log chimney at the far end from the door. Stilt cabin: the floor stands 1.5, 2.5 or 3.5 m above the ground or the water, with a deck along the entrance side (railed, open in front of the door; a switch) and a stair down that stops at the waterline. Stone keep: two to four storeys of stone walls in metre courses laid like brickwork, a double gate (4 m walls), arrow loops on the upper storeys, timber floors and stairs inside, and a walkable roof behind a parapet with merlons. The 67° pitch is offered for timber halls and longhouses too. ClaudeTools: hall options style=cabin|stilts|keep pitch=67 stilts=2.5 deck=on|off. Stone foundations under timber halls, temples and cabins are pillars at the corners, every 4 m along the walls and on a 4 m grid inside, with beams spanning them under the floor.
mods.notes: 0.12.9: The Hallwright stake is re-baked with a stricter check that the low-poly model keeps the detailed one's shape.

mods.name: Camping
mods.description:
Somewhere to sleep away from home, for the hammer (Furniture tab). Nothing needs a workbench: you make camp from what you carry.

Bedroll: a deer hide to lie on, a wolf pelt over it and a wool blanket rolled at its head. Lay it down by any fire and sleep: unlike a bed it wants no roof, but you can't sleep on it soaked through, so in the rain put it under a lean-to. It sets your spawn point while it's laid out. 3 deer hides, 4 leather scraps.

Lean-to: hides lashed over a frame of poles, open at the front. Whatever's under it stays dry: a fire, a bedroll, you. 10 wood, 4 deer hides.

Tent: wool walls on carved, crossed boards, as the old ones were. Inside it's dry and warm: you can sleep without a fire, and the mountain's cold can't reach you. It sets your spawn point. 4 wolf pelts, 6 deer hides, 6 leather scraps, 8 wood.

Packing up: Shift+E on a bedroll or tent rolls it up, and everything it cost goes back in your bag (on the ground beside it if your bag is full). Only your own, or one nobody has slept in yet.

None of it is an item: if you ever take the mod away, nothing in your bag or chests is lost (the pieces standing in the world go).
mods.notes: 0.1.7: The bedroll, lean-to and tent are re-baked with a stricter check that the low-poly models keep the detailed ones' shape.

mods.name: Bathhouse
mods.description:
A sauna of your own, for the hammer (Furniture tab, at a workbench). You build the hut; the mod gives you what goes inside it.

Sauna stove: a firebox of field stones under a heap of rounded rocks. Light it in a small room (roofed, walled all round, no more than 6 m across) with a sauna bench in it, and the room is a sauna. Look at the stove and it tells you whether it is one, and if not, why not. It makes no smoke indoors. 20 stone, 4 wood.

Sauna bench: two tiers of planks, seats three. 12 wood.

Water bucket: set it by the stove and throw water on the hot stones (E). A cloud of steam rolls up with a hiss, and for half a minute the heat works twice as fast. 3 wood, 2 resin.

Plunge tub: a staved tub of cold water for a bathhouse far from the sea or a lake. Sit in it (E) or step down into it. 20 wood, 4 resin.

Bath locker: a clothes chest with pegs over it. E puts away everything you wear: helmet, armour, cape, belt, and what's in your hands. E again and you're dressed. Shift+E opens it as a chest. Your things are kept in the locker, saved with the world like a chest's, and nobody else can get at them while they're in. 10 wood, 2 leather scraps.

Bathing is done stripped down, as it should be: no helmet, armour or cape. Sit in a lit sauna's heat for a minute (on a bench, in a hot tub, or sat on the floor) and you're Bathed for 20 minutes: +2 comfort, 10% faster stamina regen, Rested lasts 10 minutes longer, and the wet and the cold go. Bathed, you don't feel the cold.

The plunge: straight out of the sauna, within 3 minutes, into cold water (the sea, a lake, a river, or a plunge tub), still stripped down. You're Invigorated for 10 minutes: 5% faster and 10% more stamina.

Company: others bathing with you (other players, and any mod's people who bathe) make both last longer: a quarter longer for each, up to twice as long.

The game's own hot tub counts as a sauna's heat and seats, if you build a room round it.

Jarldom: with it, the village keeps a seven-day week, and Laugardagr, Saturday, is washing day. Villagers bathe in turns in the colony's bathhouse room from mid-afternoon, stripped down, throw water on the stones and take the cold plunge; bathe with them and they're company. A village with nowhere to bathe asks for a bathhouse at the Thing.
mods.notes: 0.1.6: steam from a stove that stood through a hot reload (the stove's message was registered twice, and the steam never found the stove: the bucket said there was no stove by it).

mods.name: ChestSearch
mods.description:
Search nearby chests from one window. Ctrl+F opens your inventory and a search bar with normal item-slot visuals. Type part of an item name to filter separate stacks, then drag a stack onto an empty inventory slot or a matching stack. Hover to see its source chest; use the page buttons for more results.

Default range is 20 metres, adjustable from 5 to 40 in F7. Searches loaded accessible storage containers, including chest inventories and carts; skips wards/private chests you cannot use, busy containers, creature bags, tombstones and recyclers. Up to 64 nearby containers and 512 matching stacks, with 24 slots per page. All typed words must appear in the item's localized name.

Only real chest items are moved. A drag is a visual preview until it lands on your inventory; cancelling, closing, or dropping elsewhere does nothing. Normal chest-owner permission is requested before reloading the source and checking that the selected stack is unchanged. Different occupied slots are rejected; compatible partially full stacks take only what fits. Moving out of range, stale results, denied access and timeouts cancel the transfer.

Native Linux and Windows, no other mod dependency and no custom chest save data. Install on the player using the window; native chest RPCs work with an ordinary host. Ctrl+F and Escape close the search. Mouse drag and keyboard search are supported; controller/touch search are not yet implemented. F6 removes the window and preview without moving items. Compiled and checked against local native assemblies; layout, drag behavior, live ownership transfer, other UI mods and multiplayer still need in-game playtests.
mods.notes: 0.1.0: Ctrl+F chest-search window with localized name filtering, native slot icons/tooltips, source chest labels and paging. Drag real nearby chest stacks into the player inventory through normal chest-owner permission; recheck access, range, stack identity and destination capacity. Preview cancellation, stale-result rejection, bounded scans and F6 cleanup. Native Linux/Windows; configurable 20-metre default range.

mods.name: Demolisher
mods.description:
Take down a whole building in one go, with Thor's lightning striking it as it falls. Pick the Demolition stake from the hammer's Misc tab, click the ground for each corner of the area, click the first corner again (or press E) to close it, and everything inside that the hammer could remove turns red. Press E: "Demolish N structures?" Yes calls down the Obliterator's lightning: a rumble of thunder and sparks, then the bolts strike (harmless: nobody and nothing outside the outline is hurt) and everything comes down top first, workshops last, a few each frame, by the hammer's own rules: materials drop on the ground, wards, no-build zones and chests with items are left standing, and pieces needing a crafting station need it near you (as with the hammer). Only pieces built by players are touched, never ships or carts.

Backspace removes the last corner (or reopens a closed outline), Shift+Backspace clears it. The stake itself is never built. Only the player demolishing needs the mod; removals go through the game's own network calls. Native Linux and Windows.
mods.notes: 0.1.6: The demolition stake is re-baked with a stricter check that the low-poly model keeps the detailed one's shape.

mods.name: DualWield
mods.description:
Fight with a weapon in each hand. Pairs of one-handed axes, knives, maces and swords are supported. Two knives fight like the game's Skoll and Hati; two axes, two maces or two swords swing like the Berserkir axes.

Equip a one-handed axe, knife, mace or sword, then equip a second one of the same kind: it goes into your off hand, replacing your shield or torch. You need 20 in that weapon skill (Clubs for maces); for axes, half of your Woodcutting counts too (Axes + half of Woodcutting must reach 20). Below it you are told how your total is made up. Hold Left Alt while equipping to replace your main weapon instead. Putting away the main weapon moves the off-hand one across. Equipping a shield, torch or another kind of weapon ends dual wielding as usual.

Balance: each hit is worth 62% of both weapons' damage combined, about 1.24× one weapon when they are equal, normalized against the dual move set's own combo. Every swing costs 1.3× the main weapon's stamina. Both weapons wear down. Blocking uses only the main weapon's weak block, shown with both weapons raised, so a shield is still the defensive choice. The skill you train is the pair's own. Mixed pairs are not supported yet.

Install for every player: the off-hand weapon and the dual stance are seen by others through the game's own equipment and animation sync, and the off-hand position needs this mod to look right. The damage share, stamina, skill requirement, swap key, and each kind's off-hand position and rotation can be changed in F7. Compiled and checked against the local game; the off-hand look, move sets, balance and GearSlots interaction still need in-game playtests.
mods.notes: 0.1.2: Maces and swords pair up too. Two one-handed maces (Clubs 20) or two one-handed swords (Swords 20) go into both hands and swing with the Berserkir axes' moves, with the same damage, stamina, wear and weak block as axes. Each kind has its own off-hand position and rotation in F7.

mods.name: Farmhand
mods.description:
Lay out a whole crop plot with your cultivator: select a crop, then Shift+click corners in boundary order. Concave outlines work. Shift+J plants the previewed layout as you walk through the field, within normal cultivator reach. The first edge sets row direction; spacing leaves a half-cell border and increases for larger growth radii. Green dots are within reach; amber dots wait until you approach; blocked spots turn red.

Escape pauses, and Shift+J resumes without repeating successful spots. Recover stamina automatically; add seeds or repair the tool when paused. Backspace removes the last corner; Delete clears the plot. At most 32 corners, 512 spots and 400 square metres by default. Self-crossing outlines are rejected. Plot previews and progress clear on reload or changing characters.

Without a marked plot, Shift+J still plants a short row. Shift+U harvests and replants nearby mature crops; add Left Ctrl to harvest only. Unhealthy crops get helpful labels.

Every successful planting uses ordinary seeds/materials, stamina and cultivator durability. Cultivation, biome, sunlight, space, obstacles and wards still apply. Harvest drops remain world items. BuildFromChests can supply seeds. Select a crop or seed crop, not a tree or vine; turn off BuildOrders plan mode. No extra mod is required on the host or peers.
mods.notes: 0.2.2: Keeps its place before and after BuildOrders under BuildOrders' new id (com.quad.buildorders, from 1.12.1), and still with older copies.

mods.name: Gary
mods.description:
Gary the Greydwarf is a purple forest companion: friendly, defensive, impossible to kill, and occasionally generous with snacks. Uses the game's native Greydwarf body, movement, weapons, and animation; no API key or external service required.

F3 summons one Gary per player, or recalls that same Gary beside you. Shift+F3 tells him to stay where he is; F3 resumes following. Both keys are configurable. Calls need clear dry ground nearby. He waits outside dungeons and for you to respawn; use F3 to call him after a portal trip.

You, other players, and Quad’s AICompanion characters can walk through Gary, so he cannot block doorways or push you around. Terrain/enemy collisions and petting stay active.

Gary follows quietly until a hostile creature actually damages his player or Gary himself. He defends against that attacker for up to 30 seconds and stays within a bounded defense radius. He can defend himself while waiting, including outside a dungeon or while his player is dead/offline, and resumes waiting afterward. He does not pick fights with nearby wildlife, players, or tamed friends. Friendly player/pet hits do not hurt him.

At 20% health, Gary abandons combat and tries to flee 40 metres from you. Damage cannot take his health below 5%, and native death checks are suppressed for Gary alone. He heals rapidly at a safe distance, slowly while escaping, and comes back at 90%. If his zone unloads, a saved three-minute recovery deadline lets him heal before being recalled. Calling him does not interrupt his retreat.

Gary gathers real raspberries, blueberries, mushrooms, and loose feathers into a saved six-item stash, then occasionally tosses one near your feet (roughly every 3–5 minutes). At most two pockets hold feathers; when food is available, feathers are a 20 percent gift choice. Empty pockets produce no gifts. Loose feathers must already be owned by his simulator and within two metres as he passes; player-dropped items, nearby players, bases, placed/custom items and Gary's own gifts are skipped. He skips nearby players/protected plants, never claims plant ownership, and preserves normal regrowth and resource scaling. Gifts land as normal ground items; both stash and cooldown survive F6/world saves.

Look at Gary and press your normal Use key (E) to pet him: a friendly pat, quiet forest chirp, purple sparkles, and a brief happy dance with no stat bonus. He greets you after absences/dungeons, celebrates foes he fought and your nearby victories over huge enemies, and occasionally chirps/looks toward nearby visible danger. Huge enemies make him nervous; warnings never start attacks.

When you settle near a burning fire or hearth, Gary finds clear ground beside it and relaxes. When you pause to build, he watches from the side, away from your placement ghost; walking away resumes following. His retreats choose reachable dry ground away from both you and danger, preferring cover. Combat and healing interrupt social activities. Campfire, building, reactions, and warnings have separate settings.

Within 90 metres, Gary can notice a loaded burial chamber, sunken crypt, troll cave, or frost cave entrance. He leads a little way ahead, waits if you lag behind, and gives up if the route is obstructed. Confirmed fully looted dungeons are skipped; unfinished dungeons can be revisited after a ten-minute shown-entrance cooldown. Counts unopened chest contents, loose treasure, cores, scrap piles, collectible cave materials, and removable valuables; ignores enemies, regrowing food, and ordinary furniture salvage. Reads saved chest item counts without opening/generating loot. Incomplete/unloaded scans stay unknown and eligible. Up to 512 cleared entrances are saved per player/world with your character; older visits need a complete scan. No distant locations/map pins; he waits outside.

Install Gary on the host/dedicated server and participating clients for multiplayer. The server authenticates commands and finds the existing saved Gary, including unloaded zones, before spawning. Creature simulation and gifts run only on its network owner. Uses tagged vanilla Greydwarf saves, so removing the mod leaves a normal tamed greydwarf instead of an unknown-prefab object. Special behavior and purple appearance require the mod.

Gary can ride your boat. While following within 12 metres and five metres of vertical reach, he hops to a clear deck spot beside you and stays there through sailing, turns and waves. F3 can call/recall him onto a free deck spot too. He does not take a player seat, control the boat, push its hull, or fight/forage while riding. After a brief grace period he hops onto nearby dry ground or a dock when you disembark. If you fall into the water, die, leave the area or tell him to wait, he stays aboard until you return or recall him. Injured passengers rest/heal aboard rather than fleeing into the ocean. Boarding state survives F6 and world saves; a missing/destroyed ship releases him alive. No transform parenting to the boat. Toggle Companion/RideBoats in F7.

Your Gary has a purple moving marker on the minimap and full map. If he unloads but his saved object is still known, it shows Gary (last seen) at that position; it disappears when no position is known. Only your Gary is shown. The marker is transient, does not become a saved/shared map pin, and cleans up on F6/world/player changes. Toggle Companion/MapMarker in F7.

Gary now has eight more playful habits. F8 throws one actual Wood from your inventory toward reachable ground about nine metres ahead; he chases it, carries the same normal item back and waits for a pat. Fetch is bounded to 16 metres/35 seconds, takes priority over crypt guiding and other idle activities, chases the ground landing while Wood is airborne, retries temporary navigation failures for up to five seconds, requires compatible ownership, and stops for combat, recovery, waiting, boats, portals, or F6; the real Wood stays in the world. There is no item escrow or conjured refund. A returned item can be picked up normally.

Nearby wave, cheer, dance, sit and relax emotes get an awkward Gary imitation. Shift+E on your own built wood pile marks a reachable leaf/branch nest beside it; repeat on that pile to forget it. When you pause nearby for eight seconds, he curls up there. His home reference survives saves/F6; the original pile retains normal materials, support and removal behavior. In rain he looks for a reachable nearby roof while you settle down and shakes dry afterward.

On boats he prefers a clear forward deck spot, watches ahead, chirps at visible seabirds and crouches when waves tilt or lift the hull strongly. He wears a small matte twig-and-feather crown, tiny pouch and ear feather in muted forest colors, using native game materials with emission disabled. He also greets your nearby Quad AICompanion characters, watches their building/gathering work and occasionally imitates their motions. Before a forest gift he briefly holds up a mesh-only preview, then tosses the actual stash item. These activities give no buffs or extra resources; combat/recovery take priority.

Personality activities and Appearance accessories have separate F7 toggles. Fetch key is configurable under Controls; nest marking uses Left Shift plus the normal Use key. Gary's native rig has no wave/sleep/crouch animations, so these use local cosmetic bone poses replicated from bounded activity state. New poses, accessories, nested roofs, boat geometry, F6 and ownership changes need in-game playtests.

Settings are in F7 → Mod settings, or BepInEx/config/com.bobisme.gary.cfg. Compiled and checked against native Linux assemblies, including food-conservation, injury, defense, petting, reaction and retreat policy tests. Appearance, pathfinding, audio, live multiplayer, and save/restart behavior need in-game playtests.

Reforestation: while you are near your bed, Gary now and then plants a real sapling on open wild ground nearby, beside a stump you left when he can, never in your base, near buildings, on farmland or paths. Seeds and cones he picks up let him plant more. Radius, interval and limit are in F7.

Caretaker: around home he stacks deadfall by his nest, gathers freshly dropped harvest for you, replants crops you harvest by hand (with your seeds) and stamps out stray fire. He listens to old trees, shows you berries he found, shouts Timber!, senses Omens' signs and skies, and has opinions about your trophies. Each job is in F7.
mods.notes: 0.5.7: Gary knows again which dungeon chests still hold loot. Since today's Valheim update the game saves chests in a new version (110, the same layout), which Gary didn't recognise, so every chest saved after the update counted as unknown and never as emptied.

mods.name: Meadow Golf
mods.description:
Meadow Golf: build a little Viking golf course out of the landscape and your own structures. Craft a carved wooden golf club at a workbench (6 wood, 2 leather scraps). Hammer → Furniture supplies golf tees (2 wood) and cups with linen flags (4 wood, 1 stone).

Shift+E labels a tee or cup as Course:Hole:Par, for example Meadow:1:3. Give both ends the same course name and hole number; the tee sets par. The builder can edit labels. Courses have up to 18 holes, par 2–8; use a unique number for each cup. A matching cup must be within 240 m when you start; the host can find its saved marker even outside your loaded area.

Equip the club and E at a tee to set your colored wooden ball. Stand within 3 m of the stationary ball, aim with the camera, use the wheel to choose Drive / Chip / Putt, then hold left mouse to charge and release to swing. Gentle putts begin at low power; charging takes 1.4 seconds. An amber path and stopping-point ring predict flight, bounces and rolling with the actual ball physics. The HUD distinguishes predicted range (with its sampled power) from distance to the cup. Right click cancels charging. The native swing contact event launches the ball, with a wooden impact and quieter bounce sounds. Prediction is spread across frames; unreliable results show a short direction line. Balls roll, bounce and hit real terrain and buildings; they do not damage anything. Players and creatures pass through balls, and golfers cannot hit someone else's ball. A slow ball entering its linked cup finishes the hole.

G opens the match and scorecard window using Valheim's own wooden inventory panel, recessed score area and fonts. Stand within 5 m of hole 1: [1] starts a 9-hole match, [2] starts 18 holes, and [J] joins the open match. The host checks all saved numbered tees and cups, even outside loaded areas, and names missing/duplicate endpoints or holes longer than 240 m. Each course name identifies one course: use distinct names for separate courses. A front nine may also be played on an 18-hole course. Everyone has a separate painted ball and saved card; a shared match ID groups the results. E at each next tee continues after you finish the current hole. Match play prevents skipping unfinished holes or replaying completed holes. Finishing hole 9 or 18 completes your round. [X] stops your own round and preserves its finished scores; [M] ends the shared match, allowed for its starter, the first tee's builder or the local server host. Ending hides/freezes the balls and keeps the results. [R] refreshes the host scoreboard, including participants whose balls are outside loaded areas; up to eight rows are displayed. G/Escape closes the window. New rounds replace your previous card; stopped participants cannot restart within the same match. End that match and start another for a fresh round.

The landscape matters: uncleared grass has more rolling resistance than cleared ground or built floors; Black Forest/Mistlands rough is heavier, swamp mud is heaviest, and mountain/Deep North snow slows rolls too. Clear a fairway with a hoe, build banked paths or bridges, and use real trees, rocks, walls, ramps and ceilings as obstacles. Gravity and actual colliders drive rebounds and downhill rolls. Entering native water or liquid hazards automatically returns the ball to the last shot's lie for exactly one extra stroke. A flooded tee is rejected. The preview uses the same surface rules and marks a predicted water entry in blue with a +1 warning. Preview liquid levels exclude momentary waves for stable course rules. There are no terrain changes, weather forces or damage to trees/buildings.

For casual practice, E at any tee starts a hole and Ctrl+E starts a fresh practice card, leaving your current match card. Practice replays replace that hole's result; changing courses starts a new card. E on your ball returns it to the last shot's lie for one penalty; E on the same unfinished hole's tee returns it to the tee for one penalty. There is a 99-stroke ceiling. Cup rings are visual and never excavate terrain. Indoor and basement courses use actual floors, rather than lifting the ball to outdoor terrain height.

Install Meadow Golf on the host and every player, then restart before loading a world: the club, tees, cups and balls are new saved prefabs. Mouse/keyboard controls; G is adjustable in F7. No dependency on BuildOrders or Gary. Reloads cancel a charged swing and reattach Golf's scripts to saved pieces/balls. No periodic whole-scene scans; the host indexes saved golf balls once per world/reload in batches.

Compiled on native Linux with rule tests and exact installed-game API checks. See VALIDATION.md for the current Creative test results and remaining remote multiplayer qualification. Optional ClaudeTools commands include golf status, golf match 9|18|join|end|stop|scores, and golf shot drive|chip|putt <power> <dx> <dz>. Disposable roundtest and fixture commands are limited to locally hosted Creative; they do not terraform or modify existing buildings.
mods.notes: 0.2.3: Its Claude Tools commands work with Claude Tools under its new id (com.quad.claudetools, from 1.2.2), and still with older copies.
mods.restart: Adds saved golf club, tee, cup and ball prefabs. Install Meadow Golf on the host and every player, then restart Valheim before loading the world. F6 alone is not the first-install workflow for a shared world.

mods.name: Grave Goods
mods.description:
Grave goods: the weapons and war-gear the dead were buried with. Treasure chests in crypts, caves, barrows, towers and camps (and buried treasure and shipwrecks) sometimes hold one: a real weapon, armour piece or shield, from the depth of the world the chest lies in, now and then one deeper or shallower.

Five rarities, each rarer than the last: Plain (white: just the thing, buried), Fine (green: one power), Runed (blue: two), Heirloom (purple: three, and its own name, a kenning such as Wound-wand or Battle-moon), and Saga (orange: a weapon or piece of gear from the sagas, such as Gram, Tyrfing, Skofnung, Gunnar's Atgeir, Svalinn or the Helm of Awe, with its own powers and lore and two more of chance). Rarer finds are better kept (higher quality). With the default settings, about one chest in three holds grave goods; a Runed find is about one chest in sixteen, an Heirloom one in forty-four, and a Saga find one in a hundred and sixty. Each saga item turns up once in a world until every one of its kind has been found.

Powers: weapons can hit harder, deal part of their damage as fire, frost, lightning, poison or spirit, cost less stamina to swing, stagger more, stab harder from behind, drink blood (heal you by a share of what they deal) or raise their own skill. Armour and shields can add armour or block power, health, stamina or eitr, faster health or stamina regeneration, movement speed, carry weight, a skill, or a ward against fire, frost, poison, lightning or spirit (wards add up to at most 80%). Any of them can be dverg-forged (more durability) or feather-light. Powers work while the thing is worn or wielded; their numbers show in the game's own tooltip lines (damage, armour, block, durability, weight), and the powers are listed in the rarity's colour at the top of the tooltip. Grave goods' slots are tinted in their colour, runed and rarer finds glow where they lie, and opening a chest on a find names it.

Every chest is rolled once, the first time it loads near someone, chests found before the mod too. The chance and the rarity weights are in F7 → Mod settings. Grave goods are ordinary items with a record on them: without the mod they are plain weapons and armour again, and nothing is lost. Each player needs the mod for the powers to work for them; whoever first loads a chest needs it for the chest to be rolled.
mods.notes: 0.1.1: GraveGoods.Api for other mods: Rarity(item) and Name(item). Jarldom's villagers marvel at heirlooms and saga weapons, and a pyre honours them.

mods.name: Delivery
mods.description:
Delivery: hot food, brought to you. Make an Errand Horn at a workbench (4 wood, 2 leather scraps, 1 resin) and use it (hotbar or inventory). Its menu lists every cooked meal you know: what it fills and its price in coins. Every meal has its own call on the horn, and that call is how the courier knows what you want. Blow the call for each portion (up to ten; you raise the horn to your lips for each), then the end call: "That's all!"

A horn answers from far off: your courier has heard you. After a while (a minute when he thinks middling well of you) he sets out, and you'll see him running in from the distance. He goes round trees and houses, swims where he must, and comes straight through when he's stuck. He hands over the food (on the ground at your feet if your bags are full) and takes the coins: about a coin for every six points of health, stamina and eitr a meal fills, plus a fee for the run. The fee is 5 coins in the Meadows and more where the way is dangerous (up to 45 in the Ashlands and the Deep North), half again at night. You pay when he arrives; if you can't, he takes the food back and thinks less of you.

Then he waits for a tip. Tip him and he comes quicker and runs faster next time; don't, and he takes his time. He goes from Sullen to Grudging, Steady, Eager and Devoted, and a devoted courier sometimes throws in an extra portion. He's your courier: same name, same face, every time, in a bright orange tunic so you see him coming, and on your map while he's out.

Only meals you know how to make (or have had in hand) can be ordered; F7 → Mod settings can open the whole menu. He won't come down into dungeons, and he waits outside while you're in one. Other players near you hear your calls (each player needs the mod to hear them); only you see your courier. He isn't a creature: he can't be hurt and doesn't fight, and nothing of his is saved. Settings: how long he takes, how far off he starts, how long he waits for a tip, the horn's volume, and how far others hear it.
mods.notes: 0.1.5: The horn's notes swell in slowly (breath building, not a tongued attack), with a gentler scoop up into pitch.
mods.restart: Adds the Errand Horn, a saved item with a workbench recipe. Install Delivery on every player who wants a courier, then restart Valheim before loading the world.

mods.name: Jarldom
mods.description:
A colony of the reborn, built on Valheim's own systems. Raise the high-seat pillars, take in the fallen Odin sends, give them beds, work and gear, keep them fed and happy, defend them, hold the Thing, and send the worthy to Valhalla on a funeral pyre.

Getting started:
1. Build the High-seat pillars (hammer, Misc: 6 wood, 2 resin, near a workbench) in open ground, runes to the front. They found a colony; E on them (or between them) opens the colony window. Name your hall there. They start as two lashed logs and are raised anew at each rank, up to gilded carvings lit by fire at a hold.
2. Build a bed. Odin sends the first villager once the colony's renown reaches 20 and a bed is free: Hugin tells you at dawn, and a Valkyrie sets them down at the pillars at dusk. Take them in from the colony window.
3. Mark rooms and work zones with the hammer's "Mark rooms and zones" piece: Ctrl+Shift+click on a room's floor and it's found from its walls; click a spot twice for a round work zone (woodlot, quarry, fields, foraging or hunting ground, fishing dock). Give each villager a trade from their panel (E on them).
4. Put chests in a marked stockpile room. To choose what one holds, or make it the treasury for wages, look at it with the room marker out and press Shift+E.
5. Raise a great hall (walls, roof, a door, a hearth, seats and tables) and mark it: villagers gather there at dusk, and the Thing is held there.
The hall tab of the colony window lists these first steps and ticks them off, and says what needs you.

Renown and newcomers: Odin's attention is the colony's wealth (what you've built, coins and valuables in its chests), comfort (the beds' comfort, the game's own) and deeds (raids held, feasts, souls sent to Valhalla). Each newcomer needs a little more (20, 25, 31, ... 83 at the tenth). Each soul has an Old Norse name, two traits, a trade they'd like and the story of how they fell; souls who fell together arrive together. Ranks from camp to hold need people and rooms, and raise the colony's size and how many may live there.

Villagers live as players do: they eat (three meals, from their bag or the stores; health follows food), sleep in their own bed, gather in the great hall at dusk, and shelter from storms with games and talk. They fight with what you give them (melee, shields, bows), flee when hurt, and when they fall they rise again at their bed with their own gear, then walk back to their tombstone for the rest. One with no bed rises by the pillars, slower; one who dies disgraced is lost for good and rises as a named draugr carrying their hoard. They open doors, and shut those they found shut. Hover over a villager to see what they're doing; E for their panel: mood and why, needs, skills, gear, bed and work.

Work: hauler (to the stockpiles, and keeps the fires, torches and braziers fed), woodcutter, forager, farmer (sows, harvests and replants), guard (walks the watch posts you raise), miner, hunter, fisherman, smelter, cook (cleans the catch at a food preparation table and cooks it), smith (makes what you commission), healer, scout, herder, carter, trader, weaver, gothi, skald (of an evening in the great hall, with folk to hear, the skald sings one of the hall's two songs, in their own voice, a man's or a woman's: loud in the hall, muffled and fainter as you walk away outside). Jobs come from a job board: the zones you mark, things lying about, fires and stations running low. The Work tab shows it, says why a job is blocked ("needs a pickaxe of tier 2"), and sets how much wood, stone and ore the stores should keep. Villagers fetch the tools of their trade from the stores, make their own bows, arrows and tankards at the workbench, and say what's missing when they can't work. Builders build BuildOrders' plans, mend what's damaged, rebuild what raiders broke, and pave the paths villagers wear. An idle villager plays hnefatafl, wrestles, spars at a training dummy, shoots at an archery target, lifts stones or takes a walk.

Rooms: rooms are checked the game's way (walls round the edge, a roof, a door, what's inside) and graded D to S: longhouse, great hall, stockpile, smithy, Odin's shrine, temples, healer's house, brewhouse, bathhouse, treasure room, burial ground, watchtower. Work zones have soft edges, and E on a zone's marker makes it wider or narrower. Houses of storeys work: villagers climb the stairs to beds upstairs. The colony keeps to its own ground: a neighbour's base inside its circle is left alone.

Mood: seven needs (food, rest, shelter, company, safety, faith, beauty) and moodlets (a fine meal, a feast, the hall, clothes, unpaid wages, a friend lost...) make a mood from -100 to +100 that sets how fast they work. Miserable villagers slack, brawl and steal, and the disgraced may desert. A disgraced villager can win their name back: do the deed they ask of you, or let them fight in a raid the colony holds.

Requests: now and then a villager asks something of the jarl, chosen from who they are (traits, backstory, a friend's killer) and only ever what your world's progress can reach: a trophy, goods from a land, a relic from the old dead, a starred beast killed with your own hands, or a far place seen. It shows on their hover, their panel and the hall tab, and lapses after ten days without harm. Take it on from their panel (a place goes on your map), then hand it over or tell of it: they think better of you, gain worth, pay you from their own hoard, and the colony gains renown.

The gold goes somewhere: wages every five days from the treasury (all or nothing), feasts in the great hall, offerings at the gods' altars (each god blesses those who keep a temple), coins thrown into a sacred bog for Odin's favour, a gilded high seat and banners. Worthy villagers can be sent to Valhalla on a funeral pyre with grave goods: deeds, Odin's favour and a newcomer.

The Thing: matters drawn from what really happens (beds short, wages owed, a thief, a feud) are raised day by day, each by someone it touches. Call the Thing from the colony window: everyone gathers in the great hall, each petitioner comes before the high seat and speaks, and you rule on each from the bar at the foot of the screen. Promises made there are remembered, kept or broken; matters left unheard five days sour the colony. A thief is judged as the old law had it: fine them (the bót: their next wages stay in the treasury), outlaw them for three days (they walk back in after with all they had), exile them, or forgive them. Each theft is remembered with what drove them to it ("stolen 3 times, when unpaid and hungry"): the miserable steal, and the cause may want mending more than the thief. One fined and stealing again isn't fined twice.

Raids and threats: raids sound the war horn; fighters go out to the raiders and the rest run for the great hall. Raids grow with renown. The Fulings send a herald: pay by dusk or they raid. Captives wait three days at a Fuling camp for rescue or ransom; after Bonemass a draugr jarl's barrow sends warbands until he falls; one newcomer in twelve may be Forsaken-touched, to be found by their mischief and cast out at the Thing. A master may come to teach, and Dvergr mercenaries can be hired after the Queen.

Clothes: everyone is reborn in rags. A weaver spins flax (a trader brings the first seed; it grows in the colony's fields) into linen and weaves tunics, dresses and caps dyed with berries and bark. Once Hildir is known, traders buy clothes at her stall.

Ore claims: ore lies out in the wilds. Drive an ore claim (hammer, Misc) in beside a deposit you've found (copper, tin, silver; at a sunken crypt's door for its iron, once the Elder is beaten), and miners go out to it and come home with what one can carry (about 25 ore), more with the colony's cart where a cart can go. Build a camp round the stake (a bed, a chest and a fire) and they work everything near it, one miner a bed. They go for the ore the stores lack most, and stop when the stores hold enough. The wilds are dangerous: a miner may come back wounded, or without the ore and their pickaxe; a camp and a guard along make it safer. Trips are told, not walked (the world far from a player stands still); deposits they worked out are gone when you next pass by.

Trade runs: from village rank a trader takes what the stores have to sell (amber, silver, gems) on foot, or with a cart in the colony; at jarldom rank a karve moored by the colony sails to better markets, at hold rank a longship or drakkar to the far ones. The Work tab says how the next run would go.

Out with the jarl: Follow me on a villager's panel takes them along on your travels, through portals too; they fight what comes at you, and Go home sends them back. The Expedition tab sets out with a crew, each with a role (guard, cook, scout, carrier) and packing for it; E on one of them makes camp where you stand (a fire, a chest, a workbench). With the Camping mod the crew also lays bedrolls round the fire and a lean-to over yours (a tent instead in the mountains), and sleeps on them at night.

Great works: once it's a village, the Thing may ask to raise a great work, one at a time, with BuildOrders laying out its plan for the builders. The Lighthouse by the shore: its fire is the colony's beacon and trade ships are lost half as often. The Peak Temple to the best-pleased god, an A-frame hof for the snow line, doubles that god's blessing and offerings: on the colony's highest ground, or on the highest peak within 1.5 km (pinned on your map). For the peak, set out with a crew with a builder and carriers (they pack its makings from the stores), make camp near the summit, and E on the builder to raise it there; the builder works from the camp and the carriers' packs, and tells you what to bring when the camp chest runs short.

Ships: mark a Boatyard zone out over the shore (with a workbench by it, as for any ship), make someone a Shipwright (they need a hammer), and order a raft, karve or longship in the Work tab. The shipwright fetches its makings from the stores and works on it at the water's edge a good while, and the colony cheers it into the water. Trade runs go by karve or longship once one lies at the shore. One ship at a time; you must know how to build that ship yourself.

The scattered reborn: once the colony is a hamlet, now and then one of the souls the Valkyrie brings at dusk is set down far out instead of at the pillars, by a ruin, a wreck or a standing stone 400 to 1500 m away in a land you've opened. Hugin says where and it's pinned on your map. They wait there by a small fire, calling out when someone comes near, and follow whoever reaches them home, owing that one their life. Unfound after three days, the Valkyrie carries them on to Valhalla instead.

While you're away: an unloaded colony makes up the time when you return. Outposts: a second colony 300 m or more away can be linked to the first, and a carter brings its ore home.

Moving the pillars: taken down or broken, they leave the heart of the high seat; raise new pillars while carrying it and the colony stands there again.

Running it together: the founder lets other players run the colony from the hall tab (only the founder chooses); they mark rooms, set trades, take newcomers in and call the Thing.

Installing and multiplayer: install on every player and on the server. A server without Jarldom deletes the pillars and villagers when their area loads (the hammer refuses Jarldom pieces there). Everyone on a server should run the same version: games tell each other theirs, and while two differ in what they save, no colony is saved and everyone is told who has which.

Uninstalling: disband the colony from its window first: everyone's gear goes into chests by the pillars. Without Jarldom the game removes its pillars and villagers.

Works with Omens (Odin's favour is the gods' Fate), AICompanion (beds respected both ways), BuildOrders (builders build its plans), Gary (villagers pet him), SkalTavern (villagers drink its drinks and answer your Skål!); needs none of them. Claude Tools adds the jarldom command (status, roster, villager, rooms, board, log, and test commands for single player and hosts).

Washing day: the colony keeps a seven-day week, and Laugardagr (Saturday, "bath day") is washing day, shown in the colony window and on Wayfinder's primstav. From mid-afternoon into the evening the villagers bathe in turns in the colony's bathhouse: a walled, roofed room with a door and a sauna stove (the Bathhouse mod's) or the game's hot tub. They strip down, sit in the heat, throw water on the stones, take the cold plunge if there's a plunge tub, and are glad of it all week (a mood that fades as the week goes). Bathe with them and they're company: your Bathed lasts longer. A village with nowhere to bathe minds it, and asks for a bathhouse at the Thing.
mods.notes: 0.1.202: villagers getting up from a seat in a room (the sauna's benches against its back wall) stand up in that room, not outside the wall behind it. The skald's song rides out a moment's gap (the skald a step out of the hall) and takes up again where it stopped, instead of jumping ahead.
mods.restart: Adds saved pieces (the high-seat pillars, altars, watch posts, ore claims and more) and the villagers. Install Jarldom on the host and every player, then restart Valheim before loading the world.

mods.name: Omens
mods.description:
Signs appear in the world that foretell good or bad things, and what they foretell really happens. Twenty-one omens, from raids you can avert to treasure, a great stag to hunt, a night of northern lights, and a cursed hoard you can choose to take. How you answer them sets the gods' favour, which shapes what comes next.

Every 1.5 in-game days or so, the host places an omen 45 to 85 metres from a player, away from buildings. Walk near it to read it: a message appears on screen for players nearby, a chat line for everyone, and a pin on your map. An omen nobody finds fades after a day without effect.

Bad omens:
Dead troll (Black Forest): trolls raid the nearest base that night, unless you burn the carcass with 5 resin.
Scattered cairn (Meadows, Black Forest, Swamp): skeletons raid, unless you lay the bones to rest with 5 bone fragments.
Abandoned camp (Meadows, Black Forest): greydwarfs raid.
Drained deer (Meadows, Black Forest): at night a hunting pack suited to the base's land comes for it, once someone is home.
Blood-soaked circle (most land): that night the sky turns red, and night creatures spawn twice as often, more at once and stronger. 4 raw meat softens it.
Gnawed carcass (Mountains): wolves raid, unless you leave 3 raw meat for the pack.
Fuling war banner (Plains): Fulings raid, unless you tear the banner down, which brings its three guards at once.
Drowned man (shores): draugr come ashore for the nearest base at night, unless you pay his passage with 10 coins.
Cursed hoard (most land): leave it and nothing happens. Take its coins and gems, and that night a ghost leads the dead to whoever took it.
Unlit grave candles (Black Forest, Swamp, Mountains): ghosts haunt the base, unless you relight them with 3 resin.
Scorched circle (Black Forest, Swamp, Plains): surtlings raid.
Lightning-split oak (most land): that night Thor's storm breaks, with lightning striking near anyone in the open. 20 coins buried at the oak stop the strikes.
Ship with black sails (shores): its draugr crew comes ashore for the nearest base at night, unless you light a warning beacon with 20 wood.

Good omens:
Circling ravens (open sky): players nearby are rested, and 250 metres of land is revealed on their maps.
Gulls over the shore: real fish are stranded on the shore.
Dancing lights: a light drifts off to a real treasure chest of that land nearby, pinned on the map.
Shed antler (Meadows, Black Forest): a great two-star stag appears nearby, dropping a hard antler and its trophy.
Fallen star: ore suited to the land lies cooling in the ash.
Cloaked wanderer: he vanishes as you approach; everyone nearby learns every skill 50% faster for 20 minutes.
Forgotten shrine: leave 3 honey for the gods: everyone nearby is rested, and the gods' favour rises.
Humming rune stone: that night the northern lights fill the sky: half the night creatures, faster healing and learning.

Omens that return: a bad omen left to come to pass can come back worse near the home it struck, likelier the less the gods like you.

The rune bones (workbench: 6 bone fragments, 2 resin): cast them to learn which way the nearest omen lies, whether it is good or bad, how the gods see you, and what tonight holds.

The gods' favour: answering omens pleases the gods, and ignoring warnings or robbing the dead angers them. Favoured worlds see fewer bad omens and bigger gifts; forsaken worlds see more omens, with stronger packs.

About 60% of omens are bad, chosen among those that fit the spot. A bad omen comes at nightfall when seen by day, or a few minutes later when seen at night, to the nearest workbench or bed within 1,500 metres of the sign. Raids are the game's own, with their usual messages and music, and never interrupt one already running. A world with raids turned off gets only good omens. Signs are made from the game's own models and cannot be mined, looted or built on.

Install on the host and every player. The host decides everything and keeps a small record per world in BepInEx/config/omens. Frequency, the bad chance, how long signs wait, raid reach and each omen can be changed in F7.
mods.notes: 0.6.5: With Respite installed, raid omens share one raid clock with the game and Bob's other mods: a bad omen whose base still rests from another raid waits its turn (and fades if it waits too long), and a hunting pack gathers outside the base first, shown on the map, before it comes. Without Respite the pack now starts 80 to 100 m from the base's workbench or bed instead of 35 to 45 m, so it no longer appears inside the base.

mods.name: Looking-Glass Portals
mods.description:
Looking-Glass Portals: tall, root-bound looking-glasses you can see through and walk through, with no loading screen. An old root climbs one side of each frame and curls over the arch, runes glow up the other side in the mirror's colour, and a crystal circled by shards floats above. Built with the hammer next to the game's portal (workbench nearby; 10 fine wood, 6 greydwarf eyes, 1 surtling core).

Build two within 200 m of each other (a setting, up to 2 km) and the second links to the first; one glows blue, the other orange. Or name them like the game's portals (look at one and press E): two mirrors with the same name are linked, and a name links just two, so a base can have as many pairs as it likes. The mirror tells you what it is linked to, or why it is not.

The glass shows the other side as it really is from where you stand, live, from any angle and distance, with the world's light and fog. Walk into it and you step out of the other mirror, moving and looking the same way, carrying your speed (and your fall). The camera follows you through: for a moment it looks through the first mirror at you coming out of the second, and if the second mirror is in its way from behind, it turns to a faint glow you see through. While you are partway through, the part of you that has gone in is seen coming out of the other mirror, on every player's screen, and nothing of you shows behind either one.

Shoot an arrow, throw a spear or a bomb, or drop something into the glass and it comes out of the other mirror the same way, and flies on. The mirrors are solid from behind and at the sides; only their glass lets you through, from the front. Creatures that fit the opening walk through too: your followers come after you, and whatever hunts you follows you in. Trolls, deer and fliers are too big or never touch the ground, and carts do not go through (you cannot go through pulling one).

A linked mirror hums softly, and now and then its crystals chime. You hear the far side through the glass: what happens near the other mirror sounds from behind this one, and a far land of another kind murmurs at the glass. Light from the far side falls out of it: warm from a sunlit meadow, cold from snow, nothing from a dark night. A mirror seen in another mirror's view shows its own view too.

Each live view draws the world again: about 0.7 ms a view at 4K in testing. Settings: how far apart mirrors link (200 m; the host's in multiplayer), whether the area round a far partner is all loaded as you approach, how many mirrors show a live view at once (2; more in sight take turns, and a mirror in a mirror uses what is left), their sharpness, the body doubles, the far side's light, the sounds, mirrors on the map (off at first: a pin on each explored one and a line between each pair), and the game's portal rule for ore, metal and eggs (off at first: anything goes through; the host's).

While you are near a mirror, the area round its partner is kept loaded and alive (pieces out there cannot fall), so the far side is a living world and you step out into ground that is ready. For a player who joined, the host does the same for them: it sends them the far side and keeps it moving (the host needs this version).

For other mods: a wild looking-glass (prefab BobWildLookingGlass), grown out of rough rock with roots and crystals, to be found in the world rather than built. It cannot be damaged or taken down, and links only by name. LookingGlassApi places mirrors, names and locks them, and puts them to sleep (dark glass, no link) until a player offers the right item from the hotbar or the world has a global key (a boss slain); the same is kept in the mirror's data for mods without a reference (keys bob_lportal_name, _locked, _dormant, _wake_item, _wake_count, _wake_key). Events tell a mod when someone steps through and when a mirror wakes.

Everyone in a multiplayer game needs the mod: a host without it deletes the mirrors when their area loads. Removing the mod removes built mirrors.
mods.notes: 0.3.4: Smoother near a mirror whose partner is far away: what stands on the far side is made a few things a frame, instead of raising how much the game makes every frame (up to 30 ms). The world's mirrors are looked for every few seconds, not all the time (about 1 ms every frame).

mods.name: Passenger Cart
mods.description:
A passenger cart, built with the hammer next to the regular cart (workbench nearby; 30 wood, 16 bronze nails, 4 deer hide).

It is the game's cart made 30% bigger in every direction, with two plank benches inside: seats for four passengers, facing the handle. One player pulls it like the regular cart while the others ride. Look into the cart at a seat and press E to sit; move or jump to get off, and you step down beside the cart on your own side. A seat someone is sitting in shows as taken.

It has twice the regular cart's health, and it is steadier: a wider track, bigger wheels, a lower centre of mass and damped rocking, so it rolls back upright from knocks that would tip the small cart. Passengers' bodies never push the cart around, on any player's screen. If it does go over, passengers are thrown off.

The cart's storage is opened from the cargo crates behind the back bench (same size as the regular cart's). The load pile the regular cart shows as it fills is left out, since the seats are where it would be.

Everyone in a multiplayer game needs the mod: a host without it deletes passenger carts when their area loads. Removing the mod removes built passenger carts.
mods.notes: 0.1.2: Its Claude Tools commands work with Claude Tools under its new id (com.quad.claudetools, from 1.2.2), and still with older copies.

mods.name: PolygonLeveler
mods.description:
Mark a convex polygon with your hoe, level it horizontally, or flatten it into a smooth sloped plane.

Hold a hoe. Left Shift + left click places a marker. L levels it to the first marker's height. Shift + L fits the closest plane to the current ground, removing bumps while keeping the average slope; the outline updates to that plane. U undoes the last polygon. Backspace removes the last marker and Delete clears the outline. All keys are configurable.
